subject: bachelor-level physics curriculum reference: mechanics calculus electromagnetism thermodynamics quantum

chapters.title: Vector position, velocity and acceleration
chapters.content: Position, velocity and acceleration are vectors. Velocity is the time derivative of position; acceleration is the time derivative of velocity. In Cartesian components, vectors combine componentwise. Equations of motion need reference frames and initial conditions.
chapters.source: Original Genesis educational note; introductory physics reference.

chapters.title: Newton's laws and conservation of momentum
chapters.content: For a particle of constant mass in an inertial frame, the net external force equals mass multiplied by acceleration, F = ma. In an isolated system total linear momentum is conserved. Momentum is p = mv in nonrelativistic mechanics.
chapters.source: Original Genesis educational note; introductory physics reference.

chapters.title: Calculus for physical systems
chapters.content: A derivative measures local rate of change; an integral accumulates a quantity over a domain. The fundamental theorem of calculus connects differentiation and integration. Physical models often use differential equations to express time evolution.
chapters.source: Original Genesis educational note; introductory mathematical methods.

chapters.title: Electric fields and Gauss's law
chapters.content: Electric field E is force per unit positive test charge. Gauss's law states that the total electric flux through a closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by vacuum permittivity, in SI units. Symmetry helps calculate fields for some charge distributions.
chapters.source: Original Genesis educational note; introductory electromagnetism.

chapters.title: Waves, wavelength and frequency
chapters.content: A sinusoidal travelling wave has speed equal to frequency multiplied by wavelength, v = f λ, for the propagation medium and mode considered. Interference arises through superposition when the system is linear. Boundary conditions determine allowed standing-wave modes.
chapters.source: Original Genesis educational note; introductory wave physics.

chapters.title: First law of thermodynamics and entropy
chapters.content: The first law is energy conservation: change in a system's internal energy equals heat added minus work done by the system, for a conventional sign choice. Entropy is a state function; the second law constrains total entropy change for an isolated system.
chapters.source: Original Genesis educational note; introductory thermodynamics.

chapters.title: Statistical mechanics and microscopic states
chapters.content: Statistical mechanics relates macroscopic temperature and pressure to ensembles of microscopic states. In a microcanonical description, Boltzmann entropy is S = k_B ln Ω, where Ω counts accessible microstates under appropriate assumptions.
chapters.source: Original Genesis educational note; introductory statistical physics.

chapters.title: Quantum states, observables and measurement
chapters.content: A quantum state can be represented by a normalized vector in Hilbert space or a density operator. Observables correspond to self-adjoint operators, and measurement outcome probabilities follow the Born rule. A state vector alone does not guarantee a definite outcome for every observable.
chapters.source: Original Genesis educational note; introductory quantum mechanics.

chapters.title: Measurement uncertainty and reproducibility
chapters.content: Experimental reports should distinguish accuracy from precision, propagate uncertainty when combining measured quantities, document calibration and controls, and state assumptions. Reproducibility depends on transparent methods and appropriate data stewardship.
chapters.source: Original Genesis educational note; laboratory practice.
